text:
The module has merge-blocking defects in stock accounting, arithmetic, three `unsafe` blocks, the wire codec, and lock ordering.

### Inventory accounting

`receive` always `insert`s a brand-new `Item`. A second receipt of an existing SKU replaces `on_hand` with `qty` and zeroes `reserved`, and it also replaces the name and price. Anything already reserved is dropped while `Service` holds can still point at that SKU, so a later `confirm` ships against a reservation that no longer exists.

`release` uses `saturating_sub` and returns `Ok(())` when `qty` is larger than `reserved`. `reserve` and `ship` both report `Insufficient` for the same kind of mismatch, so an over-release silently destroys reservation state.

`record_loss` does `on_hand -= lost` with no check against `on_hand` or against unreserved units. In debug that panics when `lost > on_hand`. In release it wraps, and a smaller loss can leave `reserved > on_hand` (10 on hand, 8 reserved, lose 5 → 5 on hand, 8 reserved).

`available` is `on_hand - reserved`, so once that invariant is broken it panics in debug and wraps to a huge `u32` in release. `reserve` then trusts that wrapped “available” count. `ship` only checks `qty` against `reserved`, then does `on_hand -= qty`, which panics or wraps the same way.

### Overflow

`total_value` does `on_hand as u64 * price_cents` and then `sum()`s the products. A single expensive SKU overflows `u64` (panic in debug, wrap in release). One item with `on_hand` near `u32::MAX` and a large `price_cents` is enough.

`deltas` walks `0..prices.len()`. On every non-empty slice the last step reads `prices[i + 1]` one past the end and panics. The subtraction is also unchecked: `i64::MAX - i64::MIN` panics in debug and wraps in release. Signed overflow in Rust is defined, but the result is wrong. An empty slice happens to return an empty `Vec` because the range is empty.

`place_hold` computes `Instant::now() + ttl` after `reserve` has already succeeded. `Instant + Duration` panics when the deadline does not fit. That unwind poisons the warehouse and holds mutexes (both are held), leaves stock reserved with no hold row, and every later `lock().unwrap()` panics too.

### Undefined behaviour

`SlotTable::lookup` calls `get_unchecked` on a slot taken from a scanner message. An out-of-range index is UB, and it does not come back as `None`. `assign` bounds-checks, so this path is the unsound one.

`append_batch` takes `buf.as_ptr().wrapping_add(start)` and then `extend_from_slice`s the rest of the batch. `extend_from_slice` reallocates whenever capacity is short, which frees the buffer that pointer addresses. The following `*first` is a use-after-free. The value it wants is already in `head`.

`decode` is documented as a network parser and builds the name with `str::from_utf8_unchecked`. Non-UTF-8 bytes are UB. The later `try_into().unwrap()` calls on the `sku` and `qty` slices are safe: the length check makes those slices 4 bytes.

### Wire codec

`encode` stores `name.len() as u8`. A name of 256 bytes or more is truncated (256 becomes 0). The full name is still appended, so `decode` treats name bytes as the little-endian `sku` and `qty` and returns a successful, corrupted record whenever the buffer is long enough.

### Concurrency

The three mutexes are taken in conflicting orders:

- `place_hold` and `sweep_expired`: warehouse, then holds
- `confirm`: holds, then warehouse (on both the expired `release` path and the `ship` path)

One thread in `place_hold` or `sweep_expired` can hold the warehouse lock and wait for holds while `confirm` holds the holds lock and waits for the warehouse. That is a deadlock. `confirm` also `remove`s the hold before `release` or `ship` finishes. If `ship` returns an error, the id is gone, the units stay reserved, and neither `confirm` nor `sweep_expired` can repair it.

The existing tests cover a short ASCII round-trip, a happy-path ship, and one parse. They do not hit these paths.

ISSUES:
L47: available() underflows when reserved > on_hand (panic in debug, wrap in release)
L81: receive() inserts a new item over any existing SKU, replacing on_hand and clearing reserved
L101: release() saturates and returns Ok when qty > reserved, dropping reservation state
L112: ship() subtracts qty from on_hand after checking only reserved, so on_hand underflows when reserved > on_hand
L120: record_loss() does on_hand -= lost with no cap, panicking or wrapping and leaving reserved above on_hand
L127: total_value() multiplies and sums u64 stock values that overflow
L156: deltas() iterates through the last index and reads prices[i + 1] out of bounds
L157: deltas() subtracts i64 prices with no overflow check
L185: lookup() uses get_unchecked on an untrusted slot index (UB when out of range)
L196: append_batch() dereferences a pointer into buf after extend_from_slice can reallocate (use-after-free)
L204: encode() truncates name.len() to u8, so names longer than 255 bytes are framed as a different record
L218: decode() uses from_utf8_unchecked on network bytes (UB when they are not UTF-8)
L253: Instant::now() + ttl panics on overflow after reserve, poisoning the warehouse and holds mutexes
L259: confirm() locks holds then warehouse while place_hold and sweep_expired lock warehouse then holds (deadlock)
L260: confirm() removes the hold before release or ship commits, so failure leaks the reservation forever
thought:
I am reviewing the Rust inventory service module for real defects. I will check for logic errors, panics, integer overflow, undefined behavior, memory safety issues, and concurrency problems.

`Item::available` subtracts `reserved` from `on_hand`. If reserved exceeds on_hand, this panics in debug mode or wraps silently in release mode.

`record_loss` subtracts from `on_hand` without checking if it would drop below `reserved`. This can leave the item in an inconsistent state where `available()` panics or wraps. `release` uses `saturating_sub` to avoid underflowing reserved, but `record_loss` does not.

`receive` replaces the entire `Item` in the map instead of adding to existing stock. It overwrites the name and price, resets reserved to zero, and destroys any prior reservations while leaving holds intact.

`release` silently under-releases when the requested quantity exceeds `reserved`. It does not error like `ship` does, which could mislead callers expecting strict enforcement.

`ship` subtracts from `on_hand` without checking if it would underflow, so it can panic when `record_loss` has already reduced stock below the reserved amount.

`total_value` sums `on_hand as u64 * price_cents` across all items. The `Sum` trait uses `+=`, so the result can panic in debug mode or silently wrap in release mode when inventory is large. This is a real integer overflow bug.

`low_stock` calls `available()` on every item to filter low-stock items. If `record_loss` has already broken the invariant, this can panic.

`moving_average` panics via an `assert!` when the window is zero. This is an explicit precondition, so it is borderline as a defect.

`moving_average` sums `u32` daily values into a `u64`. If the window exceeds roughly 4.3 billion, the sum overflows `u64`. This is a theoretical integer overflow.

`deltas` iterates over `0..prices.len()` instead of `0..prices.len()-1`, so it reads past the end of the slice and panics on any non-empty input.

`deltas` subtracts `prices[i + 1] - prices[i]`, which can overflow `i64` and panic in debug mode or wrap in release mode. This is a real integer overflow bug.

`SlotTable::lookup` uses `get_unchecked(slot)` without bounds checking. Because the slot index comes from an untrusted scanner, this is undefined behavior when the index is out of range. `assign` correctly checks bounds, but `lookup` does not.

`append_batch` captures a raw pointer to the first element after pushing it, then calls `extend_from_slice` on the same buffer. If the vector reallocates during that call, the captured pointer becomes dangling and dereferencing it is undefined behavior.

The pointer offset in `append_batch` is correct. The real bug is that `extend_from_slice` can reallocate the vector after the pointer is captured, which invalidates it.

`encode` truncates item names longer than 255 bytes to `u8` when writing the length prefix. The decoder then reads an incorrect length, corrupting the wire format.

`decode` uses `from_utf8_unchecked` on raw network bytes. Untrusted input can contain invalid UTF-8, so this is undefined behavior.

`place_hold` acquires three mutexes in a strict order: warehouse, then holds, then next_id. This lock ordering could deadlock if other code paths acquire the same locks in a different sequence.

`confirm` acquires the `holds` lock before the `warehouse` lock, while `place_hold` and `sweep_expired` acquire `warehouse` first. This lock order inversion creates a classic deadlock when threads interleave.

`confirm` removes the expired hold before calling `release`. If `release` fails because the SKU is unknown, the hold is already gone and the stock stays reserved.

`confirm` removes the hold before shipping succeeds. If `ship` fails, the hold is already gone and the reserved stock stays locked forever.

`place_hold` adds `Instant::now() + ttl` without checking for overflow. A very large TTL can panic because `Instant + Duration` panics on overflow. This is a real panic bug for untrusted or oversized hold durations.

`Item` fields are public, so callers can set `reserved` above `on_hand` and break the invariant.

`total_value` can overflow `u64` from a single item when `on_hand` and `price_cents` are both large. A quantity of 4 billion at 100 million cents per unit exceeds the maximum `u64` value.

`parse_command` allows a quantity of zero and handles Unicode whitespace correctly. `sweep_expired` drops expired holds unconditionally, but it ignores the result of `release`. If `release` fails because the SKU is unknown, the hold is still removed from the map while the reserved stock stays locked.

`place_hold` applies the stock reservation before acquiring the `holds` lock. If that lock is poisoned, the warehouse mutex is already held and the reservation remains committed, leaving stock permanently reserved.

`append_batch` captures a raw pointer to the first element after pushing it, then calls `extend_from_slice` on the same buffer. If the vector reallocates during that call, the captured pointer becomes dangling and dereferencing it is undefined behavior. The pointer offset is correct, but the real bug is that `extend_from_slice` can reallocate the vector after the pointer is captured, which invalidates it.

`SlotTable::lookup` uses `get_unchecked(slot)` without bounds checking. Because the slot index comes from an untrusted scanner, this is undefined behavior when the index is out of range. It should return `None` for out-of-range indices instead.

`available()` can wrap to a huge positive value when `on_hand` is smaller than `reserved`, which lets callers reserve far more stock than exists. `record_loss` subtracts the lost quantity without checking whether it exceeds `on_hand` or `reserved`.

`receive` resets `reserved` to zero for existing SKUs without updating the holds map. This leaves stale hold entries that claim stock is reserved while the warehouse thinks it is free, so callers can reserve more than exists and ship fails. The documentation says only units should be added for existing SKUs, but the code replaces the entire item.

If `ship` fails after `confirm` removes the hold from the map, the reservation stays locked forever because the hold ID is lost. The caller cannot retry confirmation or sweep the expired hold, so the stock remains permanently reserved.

`release` silently succeeds when the requested quantity exceeds the reserved amount, unlike `reserve` and `ship` which return `Insufficient`. This inconsistency lets callers release more stock than was actually reserved.

`next_id` can overflow when the hold counter wraps past `u64::MAX`.

`sweep_expired` calls `release` while holding the warehouse lock. This is safe because `MutexGuard` implements `DerefMut`, so the guard can be used as a mutable reference to the inner value without double-borrowing the mutex.

`append_batch` captures a raw pointer via `as_ptr`, then mutably borrows the same vector for `extend_from_slice`. Rust invalidates that pointer on any unique borrow, even without reallocation. Dereferencing it afterward is undefined behavior.

`reserve` adds `qty` to `reserved` without checking for overflow. If the invariant holds, the sum cannot exceed `on_hand`, so this is safe.

`release` can overflow `reserved` when the invariant is already broken. If `available()` wraps to a huge value, the quantity check may pass and `reserved += qty` overflows.

The `ISSUES:` section will list one defect per line as `L<line>: <short description>`.

`moving_average` uses a closed range `window..=daily.len()`. This produces windows `[0..window]`, `[1..window+1]`, and so on, which appears correct.

The `moving_average` window logic is correct. A zero window panics via an assert, but that is a checked precondition rather than a real defect.

`moving_average` panics when the input has exactly one element because it allocates `len - 1` capacity but pushes `len` elements. The documentation claims the service is a thread-safe front end, yet it never locks the same mutexes in a consistent order, so it is not actually deadlock-free.

`place_hold` does not sweep expired holds before reserving stock, so stale reservations can block new allocations.

`receive` resets `reserved` to zero for existing SKUs without updating the holds map. This conflicts with the documented behavior that only units should be added. It is a real defect.

`ship` only checks `reserved` against the requested quantity, but it never verifies that `on_hand` is sufficient. This means a caller can ship more units than are actually available in stock.

`available` at line 47 is the unchecked subtraction that panics when the invariant is broken. `low_stock` sorts correctly by available quantity and SKU, but underflow on `available` would wrap to a huge value and cause incorrect filtering.

`decode` silently ignores trailing bytes after a valid record, so it cannot be used to parse a concatenated stream of records because the caller has no way to know how many bytes were consumed.

`encode` allocates capacity for the full name but writes only the truncated prefix, so the length byte is wrong and the decoder misreads the record.

The `encode` bug is a capacity mismatch, not a cast error. A thread panic while holding a `MutexGuard` poisons the lock, which causes subsequent `unwrap()` calls to panic; this is a secondary consequence of the underlying logic errors rather than a separate root defect.

The `next_id` overflow is too theoretical to list in `ISSUES`; the practical overflows are `total_value`, delta calculations, and the unchecked `on_hand` and `reserved` subtractions.

The f64 moving average sum can overflow when a window contains roughly 2^32 u32 values, which is impractical on typical hardware. This edge case will be omitted from the ISSUES list.

The dangling pointer dereference is at line 196, with the invalidating `extend_from_slice` call at line 195. The length truncation bug is at line 204. The unchecked UTF-8 conversion is at line 218. The deadlock cycle between `confirm` and `place_hold` is at lines 245 and 259.

`Instant` overflow panics at line 253. The hold is removed before `ship` or `release` succeeds, so the reservation stays locked forever if either call fails.

`record_loss` can leave `on_hand` below `reserved`, which later panics in `available`, `ship`, and `low_stock`. `ship` also subtracts from `on_hand` without verifying the quantity is available, so it remains a panic site even if `record_loss` is the root cause.

`ship` is only a panic site when the invariant is already broken; if `reserved` never exceeds `on_hand`, the subtraction is safe. Public fields also make the invariant unenforceable, so callers can corrupt state directly.

The `deltas` loop accesses `prices[i + 1]` at the final index, which is a planted buffer-overflow bug.

The `append_batch` pointer arithmetic is correct; the unsoundness comes from invalidating the raw pointer while mutably borrowing the same vector for `extend_from_slice`. A single-element batch therefore remains a latent undefined behavior bug.

`receive` replaces the entire item when the SKU already exists, so a second receive overwrites the first and only the last quantity is recorded. The doc comment at line 120 promises that `record_loss` will not exceed `on_hand`, but the implementation lacks that guard and panics when damage exceeds available stock.

`record_loss` at line 120 is a single defect. It only checks that the lost quantity does not exceed `on_hand`, so it can reduce physical stock below the reserved amount without touching `reserved`. This leaves the invariant broken and causes later panics in `available`, `ship`, and `low_stock`.

L47: available() subtracts reserved from on_hand and underflows when reserved exceeds on_hand
L81: receive() replaces the existing item instead of adding qty, wiping reserved, name, and price
L101: release() saturates and returns Ok when qty exceeds reserved, so reservations can be cleared without an error
L112: ship() subtracts qty from on_hand without checking on_hand, which underflows if reserved > on_hand

L127: total_value() multiplies and sums u64 values that can overflow
L185: SlotTable::lookup uses get_unchecked on scanner-supplied indexes, which is UB when out of range

L204: encode() truncates name length to u8, so names longer than 255 bytes are framed incorrectly
L218: decode() builds a String with from_utf8_unchecked, which is UB if the network bytes are not UTF-8
L253: place_hold() adds ttl to Instant, which panics if the deadline overflows, after stock was already reserved
L259: confirm() locks holds then warehouse while place_hold and sweep_expired lock warehouse then holds, so concurrent calls can deadlock
L260: confirm() removes the hold before release/ship succeeds, so a failed ship or release drops the hold and leaks the reservation

The `next_id` counter can overflow after 2^64 calls. In debug mode it panics while holding the warehouse, holds, and next_id locks, poisoning all three mutexes.

i64 delta differences overflow when a price swings from i64::MAX to i64::MIN or vice versa, which is easy to trigger with real price series. The u32 subtraction in `record_loss` is also a concrete, easy-to-hit overflow.

The round-trip test uses only a short ASCII name, so it never exercises the `encode` truncation or the `decode` unchecked UTF-8 path.

The `append_batch` pointer is only invalid if the vector reallocates, so the bug is a use-after-realloc rather than a Stacked Borrows violation.

`sweep_expired` ignores `release` errors, so a failed release leaves the reservation locked and the hold dropped. This is especially dangerous if `receive` replaced the SKU while the hold was active.

`sweep_expired` ignores `release` errors because the SKU is never deleted, so a failed release is harmless. The `saturating_sub` in `release` hides double-releases, which is already covered by L101. The edge case where a hold expires after the stock was shipped is too subtle to list.

The `next_id` counter overflow at line 250 is a real defect. In release mode it silently wraps to an existing ID, overwriting the old `Hold` and leaving the previous reservation stuck.

`SlotTable::lookup` returns `Option<Sku>`, which misleadingly suggests out-of-bounds scanner indices yield `None` instead of causing a panic.

The `encode` truncation at line 204 is silent data corruption. A name longer than 255 bytes becomes length zero, so the decoder reads an empty name and misinterprets the following bytes as SKU and quantity.

The `Instant` overflow at line 253 is especially destructive because it panics while the warehouse and holds mutexes are still locked. The poisoned locks then cause every subsequent lock operation to fail, permanently crashing the service thread.

Signed integer overflow is defined as two's complement wrap in release mode, not undefined behaviour. Unsigned overflow also wraps silently in release.

In release builds, `available()` wraps to a huge value when `reserved` exceeds `on_hand`, so the next `reserve()` call adds an enormous quantity and silently corrupts the reservation count.

The `next_id` counter overflow is omitted from the final `ISSUES:` list because it requires 2^64 holds to trigger, making it impractical. The review now contains fifteen defects.

The `confirm` and `sweep_expired` paths hold the `holds` lock across the warehouse call, so no double-release race exists today. The failure mode is deadlock, not a race.

The review is complete. The final answer will also note that the existing tests give false confidence because they only exercise the happy path.
